body.heading: The activity with no obvious purpose
paragraphs: Play is strange when you stare at it. It burns energy, achieves nothing you can eat or sell, and yet children of every culture invent it for themselves, and adults build stadiums, board games and entire holidays around it. If play were useless, evolution has had a long time to delete it.

The Dutch historian Johan Huizinga argued in his 1938 book Homo Ludens (“Playing Man”) that play is not a break from culture but one of its foundations: contests, festivals, theatre and even courtroom rituals all carry the shape of games — set apart from ordinary life, ruled, and absorbing.

body.heading: Practice disguised as pleasure
paragraphs: The most practical explanation is rehearsal. Young animals chase, wrestle and pounce in play the way they will later hunt or flee — but safely, with the stakes removed. Human children do the same with shops, schools and superhero rescues: the adult world, practised at small scale.

Play also experiments with fairness and rules. Anyone who has negotiated the laws of a playground game — what counts, what is out, what happens if the ball hits the post — has done a first course in law, diplomacy and justice, all before lunch.

body.heading: Try it: notice your own play
paragraphs: For one day, keep a small play diary. Note every time you joke, doodle, daydream a story, kick a stone along the pavement or turn a chore into a race. Most people are startled by how much of the day was quietly play.

Then ask the oldest person you know what games they played as a child. The answers — marbles, skipping rhymes, street cricket, card games by lamplight — are a family history that rarely makes it into photo albums.

takeaway: Play is rehearsal, experiment and celebration rolled into one: the most serious thing humans do without noticing.
